problems.problem: It is known that a number $n$ is a sum of the squares of three natural numbers. Prove that $n^2$ is also a sum of the squares of three natural numbers.

Two counters stand on a line: a red one on the left and a blue one on the right. Either of two operations may be performed: inserting two counters of the same colour next to each other at any place of the line, and removing any two adjacent counters of the same colour. Is it possible, after a finite number of operations, to leave exactly two counters on the line: the red one on the right and the blue one on the left?

The court astrologer of Tsar Gorokh calls a time of day good if, on a clock with a central second hand, when going instantaneously around the dial in the clockwise direction, the minute hand is met after the hour hand and before the second hand. Which time is there more of in a day: good or bad?

Is there a finite word made of letters of the Russian alphabet in which there are no two adjacent identical subwords, but such subwords appear when any letter of the Russian alphabet is appended to it (on the right as well as on the left)?

A circle with centre $D$ passes through the points $A$, $B$ and the centre $O$ of the excircle of the triangle $ABC$ that touches its side $BC$ and the extensions of the sides $AB$ and $AC$. Prove that the points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ lie on one circle.

A cooperative receives apple juice and grape juice in identical cans and produces an apple-grape drink in identical jars. One can of apple juice is enough for exactly $6$ jars of the drink, and one can of grape juice for exactly $10$. When the recipe of the drink was changed, one can of apple juice became enough for exactly $5$ jars of the drink. For how many jars of the drink will one can of grape juice be enough now? (The drink is not diluted with water.)
A pupil did not notice the multiplication sign between two three-digit numbers and wrote one six-digit number, which turned out to be seven times their product. Find these numbers.

In a triangle $ABC$ the bisectors of the angles $A$ and $C$ are drawn. The points $P$ and $Q$ are the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from the vertex $B$ to these bisectors. Prove that the segment $PQ$ is parallel to the side $AC$.

Four grasshoppers sit at the vertices of a square. Every minute one of them jumps to the point symmetric to it with respect to another grasshopper. Prove that the grasshoppers cannot at some moment be at the vertices of a larger square.

The court astrologer calls a moment of time good if the hour, minute and second hands of the clock lie on one side of some diameter of the dial (the hands rotate on a common axis and do not jump). Which time is there more of in a day, good or bad?

Two players play on a $19\times 94$ board of cells. In turn, each of them marks a square along the grid lines (of any possible size) and colours it. The player who colours the last cell wins. Cells may not be coloured twice. Who wins with correct play, and how should he play?

M. V. Lomonosov spent one coin (a "denezhka") on bread and kvass. When prices rose by $20\%$, he bought half a loaf of bread and kvass with the same coin. Will the same coin be enough at least for kvass if prices rise by $20\%$ once more?
Prove that all numbers of the form $10017$, $100117$, $1001117$, $\ldots$ are divisible by $53$.
Is it enough, for making a rectangular box closed on all sides that holds at least $1995$ unit cubes, to have a) $962$; b) $960$; c) $958$ square units of material?

Several settlements are connected by roads with a city, and there are no roads between them. A truck leaves the city with loads for all the settlements at once. The cost of each trip equals the product of the weight of all the loads in the truck by the distance. Prove that if the weight of each load is numerically equal to the distance from the city to its destination, then the total cost of transportation does not depend on the order in which the settlements are visited.

A line cuts off from a regular hexagon $ABCDEF$ a triangle $AKN$ such that $AK+AN=AB$. Find the sum of the angles under which the segment $KN$ is seen from the vertices of the hexagon ($\angle KAN+\angle KBN+\angle KCN+\angle KDN+\angle KEN+\angle KFN$).
It is known that $a+b^2/a=b+a^2/b$. Is it true that $a=b$?

Ten iron weights are placed around a circle. Between every two neighbouring weights there is a bronze ball. The mass of each ball equals the difference of the masses of the weights adjacent to it. Prove that the balls can be distributed between the two pans of a balance so that the balance is in equilibrium.

Gardeners live at the nodes of squared paper, and flowers grow everywhere around them. Each flower must be tended by the $3$ gardeners nearest to it. One of the gardeners wants to know which plot he must tend. Draw this plot.

An equilateral triangle $ABC$ is given. The side $BC$ is divided into three equal parts by the points $K$ and $L$, and the point $M$ divides the side $AC$ in the ratio $1:2$, counting from the vertex $A$. Prove that the sum of the angles $AKM$ and $ALM$ equals $30^\circ$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_1996_0_p4_fig.png

A rook stands in a corner of an $n\times n$ chessboard. For which $n$ can it, alternating horizontal and vertical moves, visit all squares of the board in $n^2$ moves and return to its place? (Only the squares on which the rook stopped are counted, not those over which it passed during a move. Every horizontal move must be followed by a vertical one, and every vertical move by a horizontal one.)

a) Eight schoolchildren solved $8$ problems. It turned out that each problem was solved by $5$ schoolchildren. Prove that there are two schoolchildren such that each problem was solved by at least one of them.

b) If each problem was solved by $4$ pupils, it may happen that no such two exist (give an example).

Pieces stand on some squares of a chessboard. It is known that there is at least one piece on every row of the chessboard, and that different rows contain different numbers of pieces. Prove that one can choose $8$ pieces standing in different rows and different columns.

From the volcano station to the summit of the volcano Stromboli one has to walk $4$ hours along a road and then $4$ hours along a path. At the summit there are two craters located next to each other. The first one erupts for $1$ hour, then is silent for $17$ hours, then erupts again for $1$ hour, and so on; the second one erupts for $1$ hour, is silent for $9$ hours, erupts for $1$ hour, and so on. During an eruption of the first crater it is dangerous to walk both along the path and along the road, and during an eruption of the second one only the path is dangerous. Vanya saw that at exactly $12$ o'clock both craters began to erupt simultaneously. Will he ever be able to climb to the summit of the volcano and come back without risking his life?

Points $M$ and $N$ are taken inside an acute angle $XOY$ so that $\angle XON=\angle YOM$. A point $Q$ is chosen on the segment $OX$ so that $\angle OQN=\angle MQX$, and a point $P$ is chosen on the segment $OY$ so that $\angle OPN=\angle MPY$. Prove that the lengths of the broken lines $MPN$ and $MQN$ are equal.
Prove that there exists a natural number which remains composite when any three adjacent digits of it are replaced by an arbitrary triple of digits. Is there such a $1997$-digit number?
A rhombus $ABCD$ is given in which $\angle ABC=40^\circ$; $E$ is the midpoint of $BC$, and $F$ is the foot of the perpendicular dropped from $A$ to $DE$. Find the angle $DFC$.

A banker asked an expert to identify, using a balance with two pans and no weights, one counterfeit coin, lighter than the others, in a hoard of coins that look exactly alike. The banker warned the expert that each coin may be put on the pans of the balance at most twice. From what largest number of coins can the expert identify the counterfeit one in $n$ weighings?
Are there natural numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ satisfying the equation $28x+30y+31z=365$?
Can one find eight natural numbers such that none of them is divisible by any other, but the square of each of these numbers is divisible by each of the others?

The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ of a parallelogram $ABCD$ meet at the point $O$. A point $M$ lies on the line $AB$, and $\angle AMO=\angle MAD$. Prove that the point $M$ is equidistant from the points $C$ and $D$.

Some of the numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{200}$ are written in blue pencil and the rest in red. If all the red numbers are erased, there remain all the natural numbers from $1$ to $100$ written in increasing order. If all the blue numbers are erased, there remain all the natural numbers from $100$ to $1$ written in decreasing order. Prove that the numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{100}$ include all the natural numbers from $1$ to $100$ inclusive.

Several guests are sitting at a round table. Some of them are acquainted with each other; acquaintance is mutual. All the acquaintances of any guest (counting the guest himself) sit around the table at equal intervals. (For another person these intervals may be different.) It is known that any two of them have at least one common acquaintance. Prove that all the guests are acquainted with each other.

A red square is covered by $100$ white squares. All the squares are identical, and the sides of each white square are parallel to the sides of the red one. Is it always possible to remove one of the white squares so that the remaining white squares still cover the whole red square?
Having compared the fractions $x=\dfrac{111110}{111111}$, $y=\dfrac{222221}{222223}$, $z=\dfrac{333331}{333334}$, arrange them in increasing order.
Show how any quadrilateral can be cut into three trapezoids (a parallelogram may also be regarded as a trapezoid).
Find some four pairwise distinct natural numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ for which the numbers $a^2+2cd+b^2$ and $c^2+2ab+d^2$ are perfect squares.

Petya's bank account contains $500$ dollars. The bank allows operations of only two kinds: withdrawing $300$ dollars or depositing $198$ dollars. What is the largest sum Petya can withdraw from the account if he has no other money?

In a right triangle $ABC$ the point $O$ is the midpoint of the hypotenuse $AC$. A point $M$ is taken on the segment $AB$, and a point $N$ on the segment $BC$, so that the angle $MON$ is a right angle. Prove that $AM^2+CN^2=MN^2$.

In a chess tournament each participant played two games with each other participant: one with the white pieces and the other with the black ones. At the end of the tournament it turned out that all the participants had scored the same number of points (a win gives $1$ point, a draw $\frac12$ point, a loss $0$ points). Prove that there are two participants who won the same number of games with white.
Two distinct numbers $x$ and $y$ (not necessarily integers) are such that $x^2-2000x=y^2-2000y$. Find the sum of the numbers $x$ and $y$.

$12$ parties took part in elections to a $100$-seat parliament. The parties for which strictly more than $5\%$ of the voters voted get into parliament. The seats are distributed among the parties that got into parliament in proportion to the numbers of votes they received (that is, if one party received $x$ times as many votes as another, it also gets $x$ times as many seats in parliament). After the elections it turned out that each voter had voted for exactly one of the parties (there were no invalid ballots, "against all" votes and so on) and that each party had received an integer number of seats. The Party of Mathematics Lovers received $25\%$ of the votes. What is the largest number of seats in parliament it could have received? (Explain your answer.)
The lengths of the bases of a trapezoid are $m$ cm and $n$ cm ($m$ and $n$ are natural numbers, $m\ne n$). Prove that the trapezoid can be cut into congruent triangles.

In a triangle $ABC$ the length of the median $BM$ equals the length of the side $AC$. On the extensions of the sides $BA$ and $AC$ the points $D$ and $E$ respectively are chosen so that $AD=AB$ and $CE=CM$ (see the figure). Prove that the lines $DM$ and $BE$ are perpendicular.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2000_0_p4_fig.png

In a deck, some of the cards lie face down. From time to time Petya takes out of the deck a packet of one or several consecutive cards in which the top and the bottom cards lie face down, turns the whole packet over as one piece and inserts it into the same place of the deck. Prove that in the end all the cards will lie face up, no matter how Petya acts.
What is the largest number of knights that can be placed on a $5\times 5$ board so that each of them attacks exactly two others? (Give an example and explain why more knights cannot be placed.)

A rectangle $200$ cells wide and $100$ cells high is drawn on squared paper. It is coloured cell by cell, starting from the upper left cell and going along a spiral (on reaching the edge or an already coloured part, one turns right; see the figure). Which cell will be coloured last? (Give the numbers of its row and its column. For example, the lower right cell is in the $100$-th row and the $200$-th column.)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2001_0_p1_fig.png

Can one place $100$ points in the plane (first the first one, then the second one, and so on up to the hundredth) so that no three points lie on one line and at every moment the figure consisting of the points already placed has an axis of symmetry?

Six words are given:
$$\text{ZANOZA},\ \text{ZIPUNY},\ \text{KAZINO},\ \text{KEFALQ},\ \text{OTMELQ},\ \text{WELEST}.$$
In one step one may replace any letter in any of these words by any other letter (for example, in one step one can obtain the word ZKNOZA from the word ZANOZA). How many steps are needed to make all the words identical (meaningless words are allowed)? Give an example and prove that a smaller number of steps does not suffice.
In a triangle $ABC$ the bisector $AK$, the median $BL$ and the altitude $CM$ are drawn. The triangle $KLM$ is equilateral. Prove that the triangle $ABC$ is equilateral.

Lyosha has thought of a two-digit number (from $10$ to $99$). Grisha tries to guess it by naming two-digit numbers. He is considered to have guessed it if he named one digit correctly and was wrong by at most one in the other (for example, if the number thought of is $65$, then $65$, $64$ and $75$ are suitable, while $63$, $76$ and $56$ are not). Devise a method guaranteeing Grisha success in $22$ attempts (whatever number Lyosha has thought of).
(Continuation of Problem 5.) Show that there is no method guaranteeing Grisha success in $18$ attempts.
On an island, $\frac23$ of all men are married and $\frac35$ of all women are married. What fraction of the island's population is married?
The square of the sum of the digits of a number $A$ equals the sum of the digits of the number $A^2$. Find all such two-digit numbers $A$.

A circle with diameter $AB$ is given. Another circle with centre at $A$ meets the segment $AB$ at the point $C$, and $AC<\frac12AB$. A common tangent of the two circles touches the first circle at the point $D$. Prove that the line $CD$ is perpendicular to $AB$.
Two players in turn place one checker each on a $65\times 65$ board. No line (row or column) may contain more than two checkers. The player who cannot make a move loses. Who wins with correct play?

In a triangle $ABC$ the medians $AD$ and $BE$ meet at the point $M$. Prove that if the angle $AMB$ is

a) right;

b) acute,

then $AC+BC>3AB$.

In an $m\times n$ rectangle of cells each cell can be either alive or dead. Every minute, simultaneously, all living cells die, and those dead cells that had an odd number of living neighbours (sharing a side) come to life. For which $m$ and $n$ is there an initial arrangement of living and dead cells such that life in the rectangle will exist forever, that is, at every moment of time at least one cell will be alive?

There are $4$ people in a family. If Masha's stipend is doubled, the total income of the whole family will increase by $5\%$; if instead Mum's salary is doubled, by $15\%$; and if Dad's salary is doubled, by $25\%$. By what percentage will the income of the whole family increase if Grandfather's pension is doubled?
problems.proposer: L. I. Zvavich, A. S. Chebotarev

problems.problem: Devise a ten-digit number without zeros in its decimal notation such that adding to it the product of its digits gives a number with the same product of digits.

Can some cells of an $8\times 8$ board be coloured so that every $3\times 3$ square contains exactly $5$ coloured cells, and every $2\times 4$ rectangle (vertical or horizontal) contains exactly $4$ coloured cells?
In a triangle $ABC$ points $X$ and $Y$ are taken on the sides $AC$ and $BC$ respectively such that $\angle ABX=\angle YAC$, $\angle AYB=\angle BXC$, $XC=YB$. Find the angles of the triangle $ABC$.

A country has $15$ cities; some of them are connected by air routes belonging to three airlines. It is known that even if any one of the airlines stops flying, it will still be possible to get from any city to any other (possibly with changes) using the flights of the remaining two airlines. What is the smallest number of air routes the country can have?

Borya has thought of an integer greater than $100$. Kira names an integer greater than $1$. If Borya's number is divisible by this number, Kira has won; otherwise Borya subtracts the named number from his number, and Kira names the next number. She is forbidden to repeat numbers named earlier. If Borya's number becomes negative, Kira loses. Does she have a winning strategy?

The coefficients $p$ and $q$ of the quadratic equation $x^2+px+q=0$ were increased by one. This operation was repeated four times. Give an example of an initial equation such that each of the five resulting equations has integer roots.

Cut the trapezoid shown in the figure into three parts and form a square from them.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2004_0_p2_fig.png

In a triangle $ABC$ the side $AC$ is the smallest. Points $K$ and $L$ are taken on the sides $AB$ and $CB$ respectively such that $KA=AC=CL$. Let $M$ be the intersection point of $AL$ and $KC$, and let $I$ be the centre of the circle inscribed in the triangle $ABC$. Prove that the line $MI$ is perpendicular to the line $AC$.

Every day at 12:00 the share price of the company "Horns and Hoofs" rises or falls by $n$ percent, where $n$ is a fixed positive integer less than $100$ (the price is not rounded). Is there an $n$ for which the share price can take the same value twice?

a) Seven convex polygons were cut out of cardboard and laid on a table so that any six of them can be nailed to the table with two nails, but all seven cannot. Give an example of such polygons and their arrangement. (The polygons may overlap.)

b) Eight convex polygons were cut out of cardboard and laid on a table so that any seven of them can be nailed to the table with two nails, but all eight cannot. Give an example of such polygons and their arrangement. (The polygons may overlap.)

$32$ dominoes ($1\times 2$ rectangles) were laid on a chessboard in an arbitrary way so that the dominoes do not overlap. Then one cell was added to the board as shown in the figure. It is allowed to take out any domino and then put it on two adjacent empty cells. Prove that all the dominoes can be arranged horizontally.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2004_0_p6_fig.png

Find at least one integer solution of the equation
$$a^2b^2+a^2+b^2+1=2005.$$

A squared $8\times 8$ paper square was folded several times along the grid lines so that a $1\times 1$ square was obtained. It was cut along the segment joining the midpoints of two opposite sides of this small square. Into how many parts could the square fall apart as a result?

The altitudes $AA'$ and $BB'$ of a triangle $ABC$ meet at the point $H$. The points $X$ and $Y$ are the midpoints of the segments $AB$ and $CH$ respectively. Prove that the lines $XY$ and $A'B'$ are perpendicular.

$2005$ natural numbers are placed around a circle. Prove that there are two adjacent numbers such that after they are thrown out, the remaining numbers cannot be divided into two groups with equal sums.
Cut a disc into several congruent parts so that the centre of the disc does not lie on the boundary of at least one of them.

$2005$ points are given in the plane (no three of which lie on one line). Every two points are joined by a segment. Tiger and Donkey play the following game. Donkey labels each segment with one of the digits, and then Tiger labels each point with one of the digits. Donkey wins if there are two points labelled with the same digit as the segment joining them, and loses otherwise. Prove that with correct play Donkey wins.

Numbers are placed in the cells of a $3\times 3$ table so that the sum of the numbers in each column and each row equals zero. What is the smallest number of non-zero numbers that this table can contain if it is known that this number is odd?

The triangles $ABC$ and $A_1B_1C_1$ are isosceles right triangles (the sides $AB$ and $A_1B_1$ are the hypotenuses). It is known that the point $C_1$ lies on the side $BC$, the point $B_1$ lies on the side $AB$, and the point $A_1$ lies on the side $AC$. Prove that $AA_1=2CC_1$.

Nine coins identical in appearance are arranged in a circle. Five of them are genuine and four are counterfeit. No two counterfeit coins lie next to each other. The genuine coins weigh the same, and the counterfeit ones weigh the same (a counterfeit coin is heavier than a genuine one). How can all the counterfeit coins be determined in two weighings on a balance with two pans and no weights?

Seryozha devised a figure that is easy to cut into two parts from which a square can be assembled (see the figure). He claims that this can be done in yet another way. Find this way.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2006_0_p5_fig.png

Every week Vanya receives exactly one mark ("3", "4" or "5") in each of seven subjects. He considers a week successful if the number of subjects in which the mark improved exceeds the number of subjects in which the mark got worse by at least two. It turned out that $n$ weeks in a row were successful, and in the last of them the mark in each subject coincided exactly with the mark of the first week. What could the number $n$ be equal to? (Find all possibilities.)

During the first year the population of a certain village increased by $n$ people, and during the second year by $300$ people. In the first year the population increased by $300\%$, and in the second year by $n\%$. How many inhabitants does the village have now?

A natural number $N$ is given. To find the integer nearest to $\sqrt N$, we use the following method: among the squares of natural numbers we find the number $a^2$ nearest to the number $N$; then $a$ is the required number. Does this method necessarily give the correct answer?

$16$ teams took part in a football championship. Each team played each other team once; a win gave $3$ points, a draw $1$ point, a loss $0$. Call a team successful if it scored at least half of the largest possible number of points. What is the largest number of successful teams there could have been in the tournament?

A circle is inscribed in a triangle $ABC$ with right angle $C$; it touches the sides $AC$, $BC$ and $AB$ at the points $M$, $K$ and $N$ respectively. Through the point $K$ a line perpendicular to the segment $MN$ is drawn. It meets the leg $AC$ at the point $X$. Prove that $CK=AX$.

In his cabin Captain Vrungel laid out a shuffled deck of $52$ cards in a circle, leaving one place free. The sailor Fuchs, on deck, without leaving the helm and without knowing the initial layout, names a card. If this card lies next to the free place, Vrungel moves it there without telling Fuchs. Otherwise nothing happens. Then Fuchs names another card, and so on, as many times as he likes, until he himself says "stop". Can Fuchs achieve that after the "stop" every card is certainly not where it was at the beginning?

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ the sides $AB$, $BC$ and $CD$ are equal, and $M$ is the midpoint of the side $AD$. It is known that the angle $BMC$ equals $90^\circ$. Find the angle between the diagonals of the quadrilateral $ABCD$.
Is it true that to any number equal to the product of two consecutive natural numbers one can append at the end some two digits so that the square of a natural number is obtained?

A cinema has $7$ rows of $10$ seats each. A group of $50$ children went to a morning show and then to an evening show. Prove that there are two children who sat in the same row at the morning show and also sat in the same row at the evening show.

Points $K$ and $M$ are chosen on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$ respectively so that $KM\parallel AC$. The segments $AM$ and $KC$ meet at the point $O$. It is known that $AK=AO$ and $KM=MC$. Prove that $AM=KB$.

A tournament in which $20$ sportsmen took part was refereed by $10$ referees. Everybody played everybody else once, and each game was refereed by exactly one referee. After each game both participants had their photograph taken with the referee. A year after the tournament a pile of all these photographs was found (from a photograph it is not clear who on it are the players and who is the referee). It turned out that it was not possible to determine for everybody who he is, a sportsman or a referee. How many such people could there have been?

Place $9$ points in the plane so that no $4$ of them lie on one line, but among any $6$ of them there are $3$ lying on one line. (In your drawing, draw all the lines on which three of the marked points lie.)

A player has $M$ gold and $N$ silver coins. At the beginning of each round the player puts some coins on red and some on black (one may put nothing at all on one of the colours, and part of the coins may be put nowhere). At the end of each round the croupier announces that one of the colours has won. The croupier gives the stake on the winning colour back to the player, doubling in it the number of coins of each kind, and takes the stake on the losing colour for himself.

The player wants to have exactly three times as many coins of one kind as of the other (in particular, it would suit him to be left without any money at all). For which $M$ and $N$ will the croupier be unable to prevent him?

The following is written on the board:

"In this sentence $\ldots\%$ of the digits are divisible by $2$, $\ldots\%$ of the digits are divisible by $3$, and $\ldots\%$ of the digits are divisible both by $2$ and by $3$."

Insert some integers in place of the dots so that the statement written on the board becomes true.
A point $K$ is chosen on the hypotenuse $AB$ of a right triangle $ABC$ such that $CK=BC$. The segment $CK$ meets the bisector $AL$ at its midpoint. Find the angles of the triangle $ABC$.
It is known that the quadratic equations $ax^2+bx+c=0$ and $bx^2+cx+a=0$ ($a$, $b$ and $c$ are non-zero numbers) have a common root. Find it.

In every cell of a $101\times 101$ square, except the central one, there is one of two signs: "turn" or "straight". A toy car enters from outside into an arbitrary cell on the boundary of the square and then drives parallel to the sides of the cells, keeping to two rules:

1) in a cell with the sign "straight" it continues its way in the same direction;

2) in a cell with the sign "turn" it turns through $90^\circ$ (to either side, at its choice).

The central cell of the square is occupied by a house. Can the signs be placed so that the car has no possibility of crashing into the house?

It is easy to join two points in the plane by three broken lines so that two congruent polygons are obtained (for example, as in the figure). Join two points by four broken lines so that all three polygons obtained are congruent. (The broken lines are non-self-intersecting and have no common points except their endpoints.)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2009_0_p5_fig.png

Two players in turn write, each on his own half of the board, one natural number at a time (repetitions are allowed), so that the sum of all the numbers on the board does not exceed $10000$. When the sum of all the numbers on the board becomes equal to $10000$, the game ends with the counting of the sum of all the digits on each half. The player on whose half the sum of digits is smaller wins (if the sums are equal, it is a draw). Can one of the players win no matter how the opponent plays?
KUB is a cube. Prove that SAR is not a cube. (KUB and SAR are three-digit numbers; different letters denote different digits.)

$28$ coins of the same size are laid out on a table in the form of a triangle (see the figure). It is known that the total mass of any three coins that touch each other pairwise equals $10$ g. Find the total mass of all $18$ coins on the boundary of the triangle.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2010_0_p2_fig.png

In a triangle $ABC$ the point $M$ is the midpoint of the side $AC$, and the point $P$ lies on the side $BC$. The segment $AP$ meets $BM$ at the point $O$. It turned out that $BO=BP$. Find the ratio $OM:PC$.

Thirty-three bogatyrs ride on horseback counterclockwise along a circular road. Can they ride for an unlimited time with different constant speeds if there is only one point on the road at which the bogatyrs can overtake each other?

In a triangle $ABC$ the point $I$ is the centre of the inscribed circle. The points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the sides $BC$ and $AC$ respectively. It is known that the angle $AIN$ is a right angle. Prove that the angle $BIM$ is also a right angle.

In some cells of a $20\times 20$ square there is an arrow in one of four directions. On the boundary of the square all arrows point along the boundary clockwise (see the figure). Moreover, arrows in adjacent (possibly diagonally adjacent) cells do not point in opposite directions. Prove that there is a cell without an arrow.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2010_0_p6_fig.png

Six balls identical in appearance lay at the vertices of a hexagon $ABCDEF$: at $A$ a ball of mass $1$ g, at $B$ one of $2$ g, $\ldots$, at $F$ one of $6$ g. A joker interchanged two balls at opposite vertices. There is a two-pan balance which shows in which pan the mass of the balls is greater. How can one determine in one weighing which balls exactly were interchanged?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2011_0_p1_fig.png

Pyotr was born in the XIX century, and his brother Pavel in the XX century. Once the brothers met at the celebration of their common birthday. Pyotr said: "My age equals the sum of the digits of the year of my birth." "Mine too," answered Pavel. By how many years is Pavel younger than Pyotr?
Is there a hexagon that can be divided by one line into four congruent triangles?

Each segment of a non-self-intersecting broken line consists of an odd number of sides of the cells of a $100\times 100$ square, and adjacent segments are perpendicular. Can the broken line pass through all the vertices of the cells?

The points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the lateral sides $AB$ and $CD$ of a trapezoid $ABCD$. The perpendicular dropped from the point $M$ to the diagonal $AC$ and the perpendicular dropped from the point $N$ to the diagonal $BD$ meet at the point $P$. Prove that $PA=PD$.

A number is written in each cell of a square table. It is known that in each row of the table the sum of the two largest numbers equals $a$, and in each column of the table the sum of the two largest numbers equals $b$. Prove that $a=b$.
Four three-digit numbers whose sum is $2012$ are written on the board. Only two different digits were used to write all of them. Give an example of such numbers.

A grasshopper can jump only exactly $50$ centimetres. It wants to visit the $8$ points marked in the figure (the side of a cell is $10$ centimetres). What is the smallest number of jumps it will have to make? (It is allowed to visit other points of the plane too, including points that are not grid nodes. It may start and finish at any points.)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2012_0_p2_fig.png

$100$ points are marked in the plane, no three of which lie on one line. Sasha divides the points into pairs and then joins the points of each pair by a segment. Can he always do this so that every two segments intersect?

In a parallelogram $ABCD$ the perpendicular $BH$ to the side $AD$ is dropped. A point $M$ equidistant from the points $C$ and $D$ is marked on the segment $BH$. Let the point $K$ be the midpoint of the side $AB$. Prove that the angle $MKD$ is a right angle.
Rational numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ are such that all the numbers $x+y^2+z^2$, $x^2+y+z^2$ and $x^2+y^2+z$ are integers. Prove that the number $2x$ is an integer.

Numbers are placed in the cells of an $m\times n$ table. It turned out that each cell contains the number of cells adjacent to it by a side in which a one stands. Moreover, not all the numbers are zeros. For which numbers $m$ and $n$ greater than $100$ is this possible?

Vanya wrote down several prime numbers, using each of the digits from $1$ to $9$ exactly once. The sum of these primes turned out to be $225$. Is it possible, using the same digits exactly once each, to write down several primes whose sum is smaller?

A triangle $ABC$ is isosceles ($AB=BC$). The point $M$ is the midpoint of the side $AB$, the point $P$ is the midpoint of the segment $CM$, and the point $N$ divides the side $BC$ in the ratio $3:1$ (counting from the vertex $B$). Prove that $AP=MN$.

At a session of a mathematical circle $10$ schoolchildren solved $10$ problems. All the schoolchildren solved different numbers of problems; each problem was solved by the same number of schoolchildren. One of these ten schoolchildren, Borya, solved the problems from the first to the fifth and did not solve the problems from the sixth to the ninth. Did he solve the tenth problem?

$1000$ numbers, none of which is zero, were placed around a circle and coloured alternately white and black. It turned out that each black number equals the sum of the two white numbers adjacent to it, and each white number equals the product of the two black numbers adjacent to it.

What can the sum of all the numbers placed be equal to?

Call a point of the plane a node if both its coordinates are integers. Exactly two nodes lie inside some triangle with vertices at nodes (possibly some further nodes lie on its sides). Prove that the line passing through these two nodes either passes through one of the vertices of the triangle or is parallel to one of its sides.

A positive integer $N$ is written on the board. Two players move in turn. In one move one may either replace the number on the board by one of its divisors (other than one and the number itself) or decrease the number by one (if the number remains positive). The player who cannot make a move loses. For which $N$ can the first player win no matter how the opponent plays?

Vitya wants to find an expression consisting of ones, brackets, and the signs "$+$" and "$\times$" such that

— its value equals $10$;

— if in this expression all the signs "$+$" are replaced by signs "$\times$" and the signs "$\times$" by signs "$+$", the result is still $10$.

Give an example of such an expression.

Call a snake a broken line all of whose angles between adjacent segments are equal, and such that for every non-end segment the segments adjacent to it lie in different half-planes with respect to this segment (an example of a snake is shown in the figure).

Baron Münchhausen claimed that he had marked $6$ points in the plane and found $6$ different ways to join them by a (five-segment) snake (the vertices of each snake being the marked points). Can his words be true?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2014_0_p2_fig.png

The natural numbers from $1$ to $2014$ were somehow divided into pairs, the numbers in each pair were added, and the $1007$ sums obtained were multiplied. Could the result be the square of a natural number?

In a rectangle $ABCD$ the point $M$ is the midpoint of the side $CD$. Through the point $C$ a line perpendicular to the line $BM$ is drawn, and through the point $M$ a line perpendicular to the diagonal $BD$. Prove that the two perpendiculars drawn meet on the line $AD$.

There is not a single tower in the town of Ploskoye. To develop tourism, the inhabitants of the town are going to build several towers with a total height of $30$ storeys.

Inspector Vysotnikov, climbing each tower, counts the number of lower towers and then adds up the values obtained. After that the inspector recommends the town the more strongly, the larger the resulting value. How many towers, and of what heights, should the inhabitants build to obtain the best possible recommendation?

$9$ apples lie on a table, forming $10$ rows of $3$ apples each (see the figure). It is known that nine of the rows have equal weights, and the weight of the tenth row is different.

There are electronic scales on which, for one rouble, one can find out the weight of any group of apples. What is the smallest number of roubles one must pay to find out which row exactly has a different weight?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2014_0_p6_fig.png

Volodya runs along a circular track at a constant speed. A photographer stands at each of two points of the track. After the start Volodya was closer to the first photographer for $2$ minutes, then closer to the second photographer for $3$ minutes, and then again closer to the first. How long did it take Volodya to run the whole circle?
A point $E$ is marked inside a parallelogram $ABCD$ so that $CD=CE$. Prove that the line $DE$ is perpendicular to the line passing through the midpoints of the segments $AE$ and $BC$.

Misha noticed that the electronic board showing the dollar-to-rouble exchange rate ($4$ digits separated by a decimal comma) shows the same four distinct digits as a month ago, but in a different order. Moreover, the rate rose by exactly $20\%$. Give an example of how this could have happened.

Call a natural number almost a square if it is either a perfect square (that is, the square of an integer) or a perfect square multiplied by a prime number. Can $8$ almost squares follow one another consecutively?

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ in which $\angle A=45^\circ$, the altitudes $AA_1$, $BB_1$, $CC_1$ are drawn. The bisector of the angle $BAA_1$ meets the line $B_1A_1$ at the point $D$, and the bisector of the angle $CAA_1$ meets the line $C_1A_1$ at the point $E$. Find the angle between the lines $BD$ and $CE$.

The emperor invited $2015$ wizards to a festival, some of whom are good and the rest evil. A good wizard always tells the truth, while an evil one may say anything. The wizards know who is good and who is evil, but the emperor does not.

At the festival the emperor asks each wizard (in the order he wishes) one question that can be answered "yes" or "no". Having questioned all the wizards, the emperor expels one of them. The expelled wizard goes out through an enchanted door, and the emperor learns whether he was good or evil. Then the emperor again asks each of the remaining wizards one question, again expels one, and so on, until the emperor decides to stop (he may do this after any question).

Prove that the emperor can expel all the evil wizards, removing at most one good one in the process.
Can the number $\dfrac{1}{10}$ be represented as the product of ten positive proper fractions? (That is, of expressions of the form $\dfrac pq$, where $p$ and $q$ are natural numbers and $p<q$.)

$10$ people sit at a round table, each of whom is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a liar, who always lies. Two of them stated: "Both my neighbours are liars", and the other eight stated: "Both my neighbours are knights". How many knights could there be among these $10$ people? (List all possibilities and prove that there are no others.)
On the median $AM$ of a triangle $ABC$ there is a point $K$ such that $AK=BM$. Moreover, $\angle AMC=60^\circ$. Prove that $AC=BK$.
Find the smallest natural number divisible by $99$ whose decimal representation contains only even digits.

A convex pentagon $ABCDE$ all of whose sides are equal is given. It is known that the angle $A$ equals $120^\circ$, the angle $C$ equals $135^\circ$, and the angle $D$ equals $n^\circ$. Find all possible integer values of $n$.

An even number of nuts is laid out in three piles. In one operation one may move half of the nuts from a pile with an even number of nuts to any other pile. Prove that, however the nuts were laid out initially, such operations can be used to collect exactly half of all the nuts in some pile.

Replace the letters in the expression $AB^C=DE^F$ by digits so that the equality becomes true, using each digit from $1$ to $6$ exactly once. (Explanation: $AB^C$ is the two-digit number with digits $A$ and $B$ raised to the power $C$. It is enough to give one way of replacing.)

A triangle $ABC$ and $10$ lines are given in the plane, no two of which are parallel. It turned out that each of the lines is equidistant from some two vertices of the triangle $ABC$. Prove that at least three of these lines pass through one point.

$100$ non-zero numbers are written around a circle. Between every two neighbouring numbers their product was written, and the former numbers were erased. The number of positive numbers did not change. What is the smallest number of positive numbers that could have been written initially?
In a convex hexagon $ABCDEF$ all sides are equal and $AD=BE=CF$. Prove that a circle can be inscribed in it (that is, there is a circle inside the hexagon touching all its sides).

A teacher gave marks on a scale from $0$ to $100$. The academic office may change the upper limit of the scale to any other natural number, recalculating the marks proportionally and rounding them to integers. A non-integer number is rounded to the nearest integer; if the fractional part equals $0.5$, the office may choose the direction of rounding arbitrarily, separately for each mark. (For example, the mark $37$ on the scale of $100$, after conversion to the scale of $40$, becomes $37\cdot(40/100)=14.8$ and is rounded to $15$.) The students Petya and Vasya received marks $a$ and $b$, different from $0$ and $100$. Prove that the academic office can make several recalculations so that Petya gets the mark $b$ and Vasya the mark $a$ (both marks are recalculated simultaneously).

A grasshopper can jump along a squared strip of width one cell by $8$, $9$ or $10$ cells in either direction. (A jump by $k$ cells means that there are $k-1$ cells between the initial and the final positions of the jump.) Call a natural number $n$ jumpable if the grasshopper, starting from some cell, can go around a strip of length $n$, visiting each cell exactly once. Prove that there is a non-jumpable $n$ greater than $50$.
Are there three pairwise distinct natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ such that the numbers $a+b+c$ and $a\cdot b\cdot c$ are squares of some natural numbers?

$39$ non-zero numbers are written in a row. The sum of any two neighbouring numbers is positive, and the sum of all the numbers is negative. What can the sign of the product of all the numbers be? (Give all possibilities and prove that there are no others.)
A point $K$ is marked inside a parallelogram $ABCD$. The point $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$, and the point $P$ is the midpoint of $KM$. Prove that if $\angle APB=\angle CPD=90^\circ$, then $AK=DK$.

Every day Andrei Stepanovich drinks as many drops of valerian as there have already been sunny days in the month (including the current day). Ivan Petrovich drinks, on every cloudy day, a number of drops of valerian equal to the number of the day in the month, and on sunny days he does not drink. Prove that if in April exactly half of the days are cloudy and the other half sunny, then Andrei Stepanovich and Ivan Petrovich will drink equal amounts of valerian during the month.

In a certain state addition and subtraction are denoted by the signs "!" and "?", but you do not know which sign corresponds to which operation. Each operation is applied to two numbers, but about subtraction you do not know whether the left number is subtracted from the right one or the right one from the left one. For example, the expression $a\ ?\ b$ denotes one of the following: $a-b$, $b-a$ or $a+b$. You do not know how numbers are written in this state, but the variables $a$, $b$ and brackets exist and are used as usual. Explain how, using them and the signs "!", "?", one can write an expression which is guaranteed to equal $20a-18b$.

On the sides of a convex hexagon $ABCDEF$ the equilateral triangles $ABC_1$, $BCD_1$, $CDE_1$, $DEF_1$, $EFA_1$ and $FAB_1$ are constructed outward. It turned out that the triangle $B_1D_1F_1$ is equilateral. Prove that the triangle $A_1C_1E_1$ is also equilateral.

All the taverns in the kingdom belong to three firms. To fight monopolies, Tsar Gorokh issued the following decree: every day, if some firm has more than half of all the taverns and the number of its taverns is divisible by $5$, then this firm keeps only one fifth of its taverns and the rest are closed. Could it happen that after three days all the firms have fewer taverns? (No new taverns can be opened during this time.)
Find the smallest natural number $n$ for which $n^2+20n+19$ is divisible by $2019$.

It is known about a trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $AD$ and $BC$ that $AB=BD$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the lateral side $CD$, and $O$ the intersection point of the segments $AC$ and $BM$. Prove that the triangle $BOC$ is isosceles.

$2019$ point grasshoppers sit on a line. In one move some grasshopper jumps over some other one so as to be at the same distance from it as before. Jumping only to the right, the grasshoppers can achieve that some two of them are at a distance of exactly $1$ mm from each other. Prove that the grasshoppers can achieve the same by jumping from the initial position only to the left.
Inside an isosceles triangle $ABC$ a point $K$ is marked such that $AB=BC=CK$ and $\angle KAC=30^\circ$. Find the angle $AKB$.

The distinct integers from $1$ to $n^2$ are to be placed in the cells of an $n\times n$ square table, where $n>1$, so that every two consecutive numbers are in cells adjacent by a side, and every two numbers giving equal remainders when divided by $n$ are in different rows and different columns. For which $n$ is this possible?

Tom wrote the word MMO on a fence made of boards, and Huck wrote the number $2020$. The width of each letter and each digit is $9$ cm, and the width of a fence board is $5$ cm. Could Huck have smeared fewer boards than Tom? (The boards are vertical, and the words and numbers are written horizontally. The digits and letters are written at equal intervals.)

On the graph of the function $y=1/x$ Misha marked in a row all the points with abscissae $1, 2, 3, \ldots$, until he got tired. Then Masha came and shaded all the rectangles one of whose vertices is a marked point, another is the origin, and two more lie on the axes (the figure shows which rectangle Masha would shade for the marked point $P$). Then the teacher asked the children to compute the area of the figure consisting of all the points shaded exactly once. What did they get?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2020_0_p2_fig.png

A natural number $N$ is given. Vera performs the following operations with it: first she adds $3$ until the resulting number becomes divisible by $5$ (if $N$ is divisible by $5$ initially, nothing needs to be added). Vera divides the resulting number by $5$. Then she performs the same operations with the new number, and so on. From which numbers is it impossible to obtain $1$ by such operations?

$20$ teams take part in a handball tournament. After each team had played each other team once, it turned out that all the teams had different numbers of points. After each team had played each other team a second time, all the teams had the same number of points. In handball a team gets $2$ points for a win, $1$ point for a draw and $0$ for a loss. Is it true that there are two teams that each won once against the other?

A trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $AD$ and $BC$ is given. The perpendicular dropped from the point $A$ to the side $CD$ passes through the midpoint of the diagonal $BD$, and the perpendicular dropped from the point $D$ to the side $AB$ passes through the midpoint of the diagonal $AC$. Prove that the trapezoid is isosceles.

Polina has a deck of $36$ cards ($4$ suits of $9$ cards each). She chooses half of the cards from it, whichever she wants, and gives them to Vasilisa, keeping the other half for herself. Then at each move the players in turn open one card of their choice (the opponent sees the suit and the rank of the opened card), beginning with Polina. If in reply to Polina's move Vasilisa manages to put down a card of the same suit or the same rank, Vasilisa earns one point. What is the largest number of points Vasilisa can be sure to earn?

Baron Münchhausen claims that to any two-digit number one can append two more digits on the right so that a perfect square is obtained (for example, if the number $10$ is given, we append $24$ and obtain $1024=32^2$). Is the Baron right?

Mitya bought for his birthday a round cake of diameter $36$ centimetres and $13$ thin candles. Mitya does not like it when the candles stand too close, so he wants to place them at a distance of at least $10$ centimetres from each other. Will all the candles fit on the cake?

There are several children in a room and a pile of $2021$ sweets. Each of them in turn comes up to the pile, divides the number of sweets in it by the number of children in the room (including himself), rounds the result (if it is not an integer), takes the resulting number of sweets and leaves the room. Boys round up, and girls round down. Prove that the total number of sweets the boys have when everybody has left the room does not depend on the order of the children in the queue.

In a regular pentagon $ABCDE$ the point $F$, the midpoint of $CD$, is marked. The perpendicular bisector of $AF$ meets $CE$ at the point $H$. Prove that the line $AH$ is perpendicular to the line $CE$.

Note: a pentagon is called regular if all its angles are equal and all its sides are equal.

In each of the $16$ compartments of a $4\times 4$ box there is a gold coin. The collector remembers that some two coins lying next to each other (adjacent by a side) weigh $9$ grams each, and the others $10$ grams each. What is the smallest number of weighings on scales showing the total weight in grams with which these two coins can be determined?

In a certain state there are $32$ cities, every two of which are joined by a one-way road. The minister of transport, a secret villain, decided to organize the traffic so that, having left any city, one cannot return to it. To do this, every day starting from 1 June 2021 he may change the direction of traffic on one of the roads. Prove that he will be able to achieve his aim by 2022 (that is, in $214$ days).

Dunno does not know about the existence of the operations of multiplication and raising to a power. However, he has mastered addition, subtraction, division and extraction of the square root well, and he can also use brackets. Practising, Dunno chose three numbers $20$, $2$ and $2$ and formed the expression $\sqrt{(2+20):2}$. Can he, using exactly the same three numbers $20$, $2$ and $2$, form an expression whose value is greater than $30$?
Find the largest natural number $n$ with the following property: for every odd prime $p$ smaller than $n$, the difference $n-p$ is also a prime number.

A square is constructed externally on a side of a regular octagon. In the octagon two diagonals are drawn, meeting at the point $B$ (see the figure). Find the angle $ABC$.

Note. A polygon is called regular if all its sides are equal and all its angles are equal.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2022_0_p3_fig.png

At the entrance to a market there is a two-pan balance without weights, which everybody may use twice a day. The trader Alexander has $3$ coins, indistinguishable in appearance, weighing $9$, $10$ and $11$ grams.

"What a pity that I cannot find out in $2$ weighings which of my coins weighs how much!"

"Yes!" agreed his neighbour Boris. "I have exactly the same situation: also $3$ coins, indistinguishable in appearance, weighing $9$, $10$ and $11$ grams!"

Prove that if they join forces, then in the $4$ weighings allotted to them they will determine the weights of all six coins.
Is it true that from any convex quadrilateral one can cut out three copies of this quadrilateral reduced by a factor of two?

A rook went over an $n\times n$ board, visiting each cell once, and each of its moves was exactly one cell. The cells are numbered from $1$ to $n^2$ in the order in which the rook passed them. Let $M$ be the largest difference between the numbers of adjacent (by a side) cells. What is the smallest possible value of $M$?

Three distinct non-zero numbers are given. Petya and Vasya form quadratic equations by substituting these numbers as the coefficients, each time in a new order. If an equation has at least one root, Petya gets a sweet wrapper, and if it has none, the wrapper goes to Vasya. The first three wrappers went to Petya, and the next two to Vasya. Can one determine who will get the last, sixth wrapper?

$23$ boxes stand in a row on a table, and one of them contains a prize. On each box is written either "There is no prize here" or "The prize is in a neighbouring box". It is known that exactly one of these statements is true. What is written on the middle box?
Prove that in a right triangle with an angle of $30$ degrees one angle bisector is half as long as another.

Call a natural number good if its decimal representation contains only zeros and ones. Suppose the product of two good numbers turned out to be a good number. Is it true that then the sum of the digits of the product equals the product of the sums of the digits of the factors?

On the sides of an equilateral triangle $ABC$, triangles $AB'C$, $CA'B$, $BC'A$ are constructed externally so that a hexagon $AB'CA'BC'$ is obtained in which each of the angles $A'BC'$, $C'AB'$, $B'CA'$ is greater than $120$ degrees, and the sides satisfy the equalities $AB'=AC'$, $BC'=BA'$, $CA'=CB'$. Prove that a triangle can be formed from the segments $AB'$, $BC'$, $CA'$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2023_0_p5_fig.png

A guard was placed on each cell of an $8\times 8$ board. Each guard can look in one of four directions (along the lines of the board) and guards all the guards on his line of sight. For what largest $k$ can the guards' gazes be directed so that each guard is guarded by at least $k$ other guards?

The teacher dictated to Vovochka the slopes and the constant terms of three different linear functions whose graphs are parallel. Inattentive Vovochka, when writing down each of the functions, interchanged the slope and the constant term, and drew the graphs of the resulting functions. How many points through which at least two graphs pass could there be?

$12$ children, all of different strength, came to a physical education lesson. The teacher divided them $10$ times into two teams of $6$ people, each time in a new way, and held a tug-of-war contest. Could it happen that all $10$ times the contest ended in a draw (that is, the sums of the strengths of the children in the teams were equal)?

The plane is divided into parts by several lines, among which there are non-parallel ones. The parts whose boundary consists of two rays were shaded. After that one more line was drawn. Prove that, regardless of the position of the new line, there are shaded points on both sides of it.

An example of an arrangement of the lines (without the last line) is shown in the figure.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2024_0_p3_fig.png

Points $M$ and $K$ are chosen on the lateral sides $AB$ and $BC$ of an isosceles acute-angled triangle $ABC$. The segments $CM$ and $AK$ meet at the point $E$. It turned out that $\angle MEA=\angle ABC$. Prove that the midpoints of all possible segments $MK$ lie on one line.

$9$ vertical posts stand in a row. At some places between neighbouring posts horizontal sticks are inserted, no two of which are at the same height. A beetle crawls from bottom to top; when it meets a stick, it crawls along it to the neighbouring post and continues to crawl upwards. It is known that if the beetle starts at the bottom of the first post, it finishes its way on the ninth post. Is it always possible to remove one of the sticks so that the beetle, starting at the bottom of the first post, ends up at the top of the fifth post?

For example, if the sticks are arranged as in the figure, the beetle will crawl along the solid line. If the third stick on the beetle's path is removed, it will crawl along the dashed line.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2024_0_p5_fig.png

Vasya chose $100$ distinct natural numbers from the set $1, 2, 3, \ldots, 120$ and placed them in some order in place of the asterisks in the expression ($100$ asterisks and $50$ root signs in all)
$$\sqrt{(*+*)\cdot\sqrt{(*+*)\cdot\sqrt{\ldots\sqrt{*+*}}}}.$$
Could the value of the resulting expression be an integer?

Two natural numbers are written on the board, one of which is obtained from the other by a permutation of its digits. Can their difference equal $2025$? (The notation of a natural number cannot begin with zero.)

$12$ participants, not all of them liars and not all of them truth-lovers, gathered at a joint symposium of liars (who always lie) and truth-lovers (who always tell the truth). Every two participants are either acquainted or unacquainted with each other. Each of them answered "yes" or "no" to the question "Are you acquainted?" about each of the others. What is the smallest number of "yes" answers that could have been received?
In a triangle $ABC$ a point $D$ (different from $A$ and $B$) is marked on the side $AB$, and the median $AM$ is drawn. It turned out that $AM=\frac12CD$. Must the triangle $ABC$ be obtuse-angled?

Can an infinite number of chess knights be placed on the infinite squared plane (at most one knight per cell) so that each knight attacks exactly $5$ others?

Recall that a chess knight attacks $8$ cells, as shown in the figure.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo8_2025_0_p4_fig.png

$50$ numbers (not necessarily integers) stand around a circle. It is known that the product of any $25$ of the numbers differs from the product of the remaining $25$ by at most $2$. Prove that some two neighbouring numbers differ by at most $2$.

An equilateral triangle is cut into triangles each of which is either right-angled or isosceles. All the right triangles are congruent to each other, and all the isosceles ones are too. Must all the angles of the isosceles triangles be multiples of $30^\circ$?

Alice wrote down positive numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $e$ (not necessarily integers), and Marusya the numbers $\frac1a$, $\frac1b$, $\frac1c$, $\frac1d$, $\frac1e$. It turned out that the sum of Alice's numbers is greater than the sum of Marusya's numbers. Could the product of Alice's numbers be smaller than the product of Marusya's numbers?

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ a point $E$ was chosen on the altitude $BD$ inside the triangle. The point $K$ is the midpoint of the segment $AE$, and the point $L$ is the midpoint of the segment $BC$. It turned out that the points $K$, $D$, $L$ are consecutive vertices of a square. Prove that the fourth vertex of the square lies on the line $AB$.

Polina wrote down a number ending in $2026$. And Styopa computed the sum of all the natural divisors of this number (including $1$ and the number itself). Could he have obtained the number $1\,000\,000\,001$?

The king decided to test his court sage. He laid out $144$ gold coins identical in appearance in the form of a $12\times 12$ square and announced that among them there are exactly $12$ counterfeit coins, which lie in a line (horizontal or vertical). All the genuine coins weigh the same, while the counterfeit ones may weigh differently, but each of them is lighter than a genuine one. The king asks to find $110$ genuine coins in two weighings on a balance with two pans and no weights. Can the sage act so as to be sure to cope with the king's task?

A pan balance shows which of the two pans holds the heavier load. If the loads weigh the same, the balance shows equality. Any number of coins may be put on each pan.

Inside an isosceles triangle $ABC$ ($AB=AC$) a point $D$ is chosen so that $AD=BC$, $\angle DAB=\angle DBC$. The point $K$ on the segment $BD$ is such that $\angle AKD=60^\circ$. The points $K$ and $B$ are different. Prove that $\angle BAK=2\angle KAD$.

A council consists of $n\geqslant 5$ elves, each of whom trusts one or several other elves (trust is not necessarily mutual). They want one of the elves to take the Ring of Power, after which the current holder of the Ring passes it to one of those whom he trusts. It is known that in this way the Ring can pass (not necessarily directly) from any elf to any other. The elves want to act so that as a result of $k$ passes of the Ring it has been at least once with each elf. For what smallest $k$ (for given $n$) will they certainly succeed in doing this (regardless of who trusts whom)?
